title: Iestyn and Rascal's Upside-Down Map
markdown:
Once, in a cozy little dell where sunshine dappled through the leaves and buttercups nodded hello like cheerful little friends, lived a bunny named Iestyn and a rat named Rascal. Iestyn was a bunny of remarkable neatness. His whiskers were always brushed until they gleamed, his burrow was as tidy as a perfectly arranged bouquet of wildflowers, and his carrot crunchies were stacked in perfect little pyramids, each one identical to the last. He liked things just so. Rascal, on the other hand, was a rat of magnificent mischief and boundless curiosity. His fur was often a little ruffled from exploring the nooks and crannies of the dell, his nose was always twitching, catching exciting new scents, and he firmly believed a little bit of cheese crumb, or perhaps a forgotten berry, never hurt anyone, especially if it was discovered in a secret hidden place.

These two did not always see eye to eye. Their very natures were like two different songs, one a gentle hum and the other a lively jig. Iestyn liked things planned. “We shall have a perfectly portioned breakfast of dewdrop-kissed clover at precisely seven o’clock,” he’d declare, smoothing his already-smooth fur. “And then, at eight, we shall organize the pebble collection by size and colour.”

Rascal liked things surprising. “Surprising is the best kind of breakfast!” he’d squeak, already halfway into a discarded acorn shell, eyes sparkling with the thrill of the unknown. “And pebble organizing? Sounds like something that happens when the sun is asleep.”

One breezy morning, while they were grumbling softly over who had borrowed whose favourite daisy chain (Iestyn insisted it was his, Rascal swore he’d only admired it), a crinkly folded piece of parchment fluttered down from the sky. It landed right between them with a gentle whumpf, a little whisper from the wind itself.

“Ooh, a map!” squeaked Rascal, little whiskers quivering. His bright beady eyes sparkled.

“A map?” sniffed Iestyn, nudging it with a careful clean paw. He smoothed it down, trying to make the creases lie flat. “It looks rather unorganized and a bit grubby.” He did not like things being grubby.

This was no ordinary map. It was a map to the legendary Berry-Bounty Picnic Spot, a place whispered about by the chattering squirrels and sung about in happy little tunes by the field mice. It was said to be a haven bursting with the juiciest plumpest berries, the sweetest most tender clover, and the crunchiest most delicious nuts imaginable. A place where a picnic would be truly, wonderfully magnificent.

And wouldn’t you know it, this crinkly parchment showed the way.

“I’ll hold the map,” declared Iestyn, puffing out his fluffy chest. “My paws are the steadiest, and I can follow a straight line without wavering.”

“Nonsense!” chattered Rascal, bouncing on his hind legs. “My eyes are the sharpest. I can spot a hidden path or a funny-shaped cloud from a mile away. I’ll hold it.”

And so began the bickering. Oh, the bickering. It was a lively chorus of squeaks and sniffles, of ruffled fur and indignant thumps. Iestyn insisted they go left at the big friendly oak tree. Rascal was absolutely, positively certain it was right. They tugged and they pulled, their little noses practically bumping as they argued over which way was the right way. The map, caught between them, crinkled and threatened to tear.

“My whiskers say left!” declared Iestyn with a determined twitch. “They are excellent at sensing direction, you know.”

“My tail says right!” countered Rascal, wagging it with all his might. “It has a special wiggle for adventure this way.”

Professor Hoot, a wise old owl who lived in the very oak tree they were squabbling under, blinked one sleepy golden eye. He ruffled his feathers and let out a soft thoughtful sound. “Hoo-hoo. The best journeys are often shared with understanding, not arguments.” But neither Iestyn nor Rascal were listening. They were far too busy being cross with each other.

Finally, with a huff and a puff from Iestyn and a determined squeak from Rascal, they agreed to try Rascal’s way. They stomped off, the map clutched tightly between them, each one still convinced they knew best. They followed the squiggly line on the map, their paws pattering through a field of giggling daisies that seemed to rustle with laughter as they passed. A grumpy badger snuffled loudly from a nearby bush, making them jump. “A growling beast!” squeaked Rascal, and they scurried behind a thick holly bush, hearts thumping like tiny drums, the earthy smell of damp leaves filling their noses.

Then they hopped over a bubbling brook that tickled their toes with its cool spray, and ventured into a whispering willow wood, where the long green leaves brushed their ears like gentle secrets. They spotted a patch of plump inviting berries and raced towards them, tummies rumbling with hunger. But when they got there, the berries shimmered and vanished. It was only the sunbeams dancing on the dewdrops, playing a trick on their eyes.

“This must be it!” declared Rascal, pointing a triumphant paw at a patch of rather droopy ordinary-looking mushrooms. “The map shows a mushroomy place right here.”

Iestyn squinted, bright eyes scanning the drawing. “But it also shows a very tall, spiky thing,” he mused, pointing at a peculiar sketch. “That doesn’t look like a mushroom at all. It looks more like a pointy hat.”

Then Rascal peered closer. And Iestyn peered closer, nose twitching with concentration. And as they did, a funny fluttery feeling started to bubble in their tummies. The little drawings of trees seemed to be pointing downwards, and the path lines seemed to be leading the wrong way up, as if the map had been printed upside down.

“Hmm,” said Iestyn, long ears drooping just a tiny bit. He looked from the map to the woods, a thoughtful frown on his furry brow. “That’s the curious thing about maps, Rascal. Sometimes they’re not always right side up when you find them.”

Rascal’s jaw dropped open with a little squeak. “Upside down?” he repeated, voice a tiny whisper. “We’ve been going the wrong way all along? We’ve been hopping and scampering in the wrong direction?”

And they had. They had followed the map upside down, convinced of their own rightness, and now they were very, very lost. The giggling daisies had fallen silent, their cheerful rustle replaced by a quiet sigh. The whispering willows seemed to droop with disappointment, their leaves no longer sharing secrets but murmuring worries. And the sun, which had been so cheerful and bright, was starting to dip low in the sky, painting the clouds in soft sleepy colours. The woods felt very, very big and very, very dark, and the idea of being there all night gave Iestyn a little shiver, a cold lonely shiver.

Their tummies rumbled, not with the happy hunger for berries and nuts, but with the hollow ache of loneliness and regret. Iestyn missed his neat predictable burrow, where everything was in its proper place. Rascal missed his happy-go-lucky explorations, but even more, he missed the easy laughter he usually shared with Iestyn, and he certainly missed not having to argue all the time. They sat down, a little heap of gloom under the shade of a tall unyielding fern.

“I’m sorry I was so stubborn, Rascal,” whispered Iestyn, voice barely audible above the rustling leaves. His nose twitched sadly.

“Me too, Iestyn,” mumbled Rascal, kicking a small grey pebble with his toe. “I just really wanted to be right about the path.”

“But being right isn’t as much fun as being happy together, is it?” said Iestyn softly. He looked around, sharp bunny eyes scanning the familiar yet suddenly strange landscape. And then he saw it. A single plump raspberry bush, its berries a deep inviting ruby red, gleaming even in the fading light. “Wait a minute!” he exclaimed, ears perking up slightly. “This bush—this very bush. It only grows near our dell. I remember it.”

Rascal perked up too, whiskers twitching with renewed interest. He remembered a little squiggle on the map, a wavy line near a bunch of little dots that Iestyn had dismissed as unnecessary scribbles. “And that wavy line!” he chirped, voice gaining a little of its usual bounce. “I thought it was a wiggly worm, but it looks just like the brook. The brook we hopped over.”

And just like that, with a shared look and a quiet understanding passing between them, they turned the map. And wouldn’t you know it, there it was, clear as day: the Berry-Bounty Picnic Spot, just a hop and a skip away, right where the brook met the raspberry bushes. A little red X marked the perfect spot.

Their hearts did a little somersault of pure joy. They scampered to the spot, and oh, it was even more wonderful than the whispers and songs had described. Berries plump and juicy, like little jewels. Clover sweet and tender, the most delicious green you ever did see. And nuts, oh so many nuts, crunchy and plentiful. They sat down, side by side, and for the first time that day they shared a genuine happy smile.

Iestyn nudged the biggest reddest berry he could find towards Rascal. Rascal, in turn, nudged a perfect shiny acorn towards Iestyn. They munched and they crunched, and the grumbles and worries melted away like dew in the morning sunshine. The adventure, though a little bumpy, had led them to a wonderful treasure.

And as the last sweet berry was shared, and the sun painted the sky in hues of glorious orange and soft pink, Iestyn the bunny and Rascal the rat knew something important. That’s the curious thing about adventures: they’re always better, and the treasures always sweeter, when you share them with a friend, even a friend who likes to go right when you prefer left, and even if the map is a bit tricky.
